subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (1, 2) and (3, 4), B is the matrix with rows (3, 8) and (7, 2), and 2X + A = B, then find X.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find X from this matrix equation.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Rearrange and subtract
steps.margin_note: First mark. Treat it like an ordinary equation: move A across, then deal with the 2. B − A is an entry-by-entry subtraction.
steps.memory_tip: Treat it like an ordinary equation: move A across, then deal with the 2.

recall.must_convey: That the equation is rearranged to 2X = B − A and the subtraction done entry by entry.
accept: rearrange to two X equals B minus A then subtract entry by entry
move A to the other side so two X is B minus A
take A away from B to get two X
A ni other side ki teeste two X equals B minus A avthundi
first make it two X equals B minus A and subtract

steps.why: Matrix equations rearrange exactly like number equations for addition and subtraction. It is only multiplication where the rules differ.
common_mistakes: Computing A − B instead of B − A.
Trying to divide B by A, which is not a matrix operation.

steps.label: Divide by 2
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Dividing a matrix by 2 halves EVERY entry, including the negative one: −2 becomes −1.
steps.memory_tip: Dividing a matrix by 2 halves EVERY entry, the negative one included.

recall.must_convey: That every entry of the matrix is divided by 2, giving X with rows (1, 3) and (2, −1).
accept: divide every entry by two to get one three two minus one
halve each entry so X is one three and two minus one
divide the whole matrix by two
prathi entry ni two tho divide cheste X vasthundi
X has rows one three and two minus one

steps.why: Dividing by a scalar reaches every entry, the same way multiplying does. Missing one entry is the only way to get this step wrong.

insider_note: Rearrange to 2X = B − A before dividing, and keep the order B − A. Every entry is then halved, which is what makes the answer come out in whole numbers.
